auditedPrs.notes: Audited squash commit 719aa88 on main against github.com/tailscale/tailscale at e2ed432399c9b0fda7aa14e9eb27784d2d893c55, the pin in PORTING.md, fetched with depth 1. The PR cites no Go file. It bounds the netstack's ingress pipe at 4096 packets and 4096 * MTU bytes, drops what does not fit with try_send, and leaves egress unbounded. The closest upstream code is wgengine/netstack: link_endpoint.go and netstack.go. Upstream has no ingress queue. Inbound packets reach gVisor synchronously: injectInbound -> linkEndpoint.gro -> injectInbound -> DeliverNetworkPacket. So a fast peer is slowed by backpressure into the WireGuard receive path, not by a drop-tail ring. Dropping is a fair stand-in for that backpressure here, because this tree's dataplane-to-transport channel is unbounded and upstream's netstack also drops silently when it is not ready. The ingress change itself therefore has no behavioural divergence worth filing. The 4096 depth and the MTU-based byte budget are this tree's own numbers. Upstream has no ingress number to match. Upstream does bound the other direction, and that is the one finding. The seven new tests call the production code: WakingPipe::ingress_bounded, try_send, WakingPipeDev::receive/transmit, piped_ingress_bounded and pump_ingress. All seven passed in the gate run.

gate.detail: Ran the scoped gate stages on main 719aa88 with CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=4, RUST_TEST_THREADS=4 and TS_RS_EXPERIMENT set. All stages exited 0. 1) cargo run -p checks. 2) cargo clippy --workspace --exclude ts_cli_util --lib --no-deps --all-features -- -D warnings. 3) The same clippy over bins/tests/benches/examples with -D warnings -A missing_docs. 4) cargo nextest run -p geiserx_ts_control -p geiserx_ts_runtime -p geiserx_ts_netstack_smoltcp --all-features --no-fail-fast: 998 run, 998 passed, 3 skipped, in 61.6s. 5) cargo build --workspace --exclude ts_cli_util --all-targets --all-features. ts_netstack_smoltcp was added to the nextest scope because #587 adds tests there. The 3 skipped tests were filtered out on purpose because they need sockets this environment blocks. serve_path_proxy_replays_consumed_head_to_backend and proxy_with_prefix_writes_prefix_before_bidi_copy hang on a dropped loopback SYN, and probe_stun_servers_once_sends_binding_request needs outbound UDP. The full bin/check was not run, for two reasons. ts_cli_util's tracy feature does not compile under --all-features. And cargo deny check all refuses aws-lc-rs/aws-lc-sys on every branch, so the set -e script stops before nextest.

findings.title: Netstack egress stays unbounded, but upstream bounds its outbound link-endpoint queues at 512 packets with backpressure
findings.detail: Upstream builds its netstack link endpoint with newLinkEndpoint(512, ...) (wgengine/netstack/netstack.go:413). That gives each outbound queue a 512-slot channel (link_endpoint.go newLinkEndpoint), and queue.Write blocks when the channel is full. gVisor's WritePackets therefore pushes back on the stack when the consumer is slow, and the send side cannot pile up packets without limit. #587 makes WakingPipe::ingress_bounded build the device-to-caller direction with flume::unbounded(). The test egress_is_not_bounded pins that choice. The stated reason is that smoltcp's TxToken::consume cannot wait. So egress from both the application netstack and the forwarder netstack has no cap on packets or bytes. If the dataplane drains slower than smoltcp emits, the queue grows without limit. Examples are UDP replies relayed back to a peer through an exit node, or retransmission bursts. Upstream bounds this case and #587 does not. The PR's framing ('Egress stays unbounded so smoltcp never blocks its poll loop') records the choice but does not port upstream's bound. A faithful port needs some limit on egress. One option is to stop offering a TxToken from Device::transmit while the egress queue is full, which pushes back like upstream does without blocking inside consume.
